uses defence mechanisms to reduce conflict/anxiety.","dep":[],"ft":false,"essentialTerms":["reality principle","mediates/balances"],"allow":["'executive of personality'","conscious part","defence mechanisms to protect from anxiety"],"reject":["ego as moral guide (that is superego)"]},{"id":"5","marks":1,"code":"AO1","text":"Superego: develops around age 5 (after phallic stage/resolution of Oedipus complex), internalised morals/standards from same-sex parent; a healthy personality requires a balanced compromise; imbalance (e.g. dominant id or punitive superego) leads to psychological disorder.","dep":["3","4","5"],"ft":false,"essentialTerms":["conflict/dynamic between structures"],"allow":["tripartite structure interacting to form personality","imbalance linked to disorder e.g. weak ego"],"reject":["structures described in isolation with no link/conflict"]}]},"answer":"Six AO1 marks for accurate knowledge of the unconscious and the tripartite personality structure. Award one mark per point; points 2 and 6 are dependent as indicated.","acceptableAlternatives":["Point 1: 'the unconscious is thoughts/memories we are unaware of that still affect behaviour' scores the mark without the word 'repressed'","Point 2: any valid illustration of unconscious influence (dreams, slips, humour, symptoms) gains the mark","Point 4: 'mediator/referee between id and superego' accepted for 'mediates'","Point 6: 'the three parts interact/conflict and the outcome shapes personality' accepted without the word 'dynamic'"],"commonMistakes":["Describing defence mechanisms in detail instead of the structure of personality","Confusing ego and superego functions (ego as moral guide)","Stating the superego is present at birth","Listing the three parts with no explanation of principles (pleasure/reality/morality)","Treating the unconscious as merely 'not currently thinking' rather than a hidden store influencing behaviour"]},{"questionId":"q16","maxMarks":12,"marking":{"type":"banded","bands":[{"id":"B4","min":10,"max":12,"descriptor":"Thorough, accurate and well-organised knowledge of the cognitive approach: assumptions (internal mental processes studied indirectly; mind as 'computer'; schema), theoretical/inference-based models (e.g. multi-store model, working memory model, cognitive priming or Beck/Ellis applied as cognitive frameworks) and emergence of cognitive neuroscience. Evaluation is effective and balanced, with at least two well-developed evaluation points that may include comparison with other approaches (e.g. soft determinism vs hard determinism of behaviourist approach; machine reductionism vs holism of humanistic approach; greater scientific rigour than psychodynamic approach; less ecologically valid than humanistic/holistic approaches; application to AI and CBT). Discussion is sustained, uses accurate terminology and reaches a reasoned conclusion or clear overall judgement.","examples":"e.g. Accurate description of schema as mental frameworks that organise and interpret information, with illustration (e.g. baby schema for sucking/grasping); clear explanation of inference from observable behaviour to internal processes; evaluation comparing cognitive approach's soft determinism with the behaviourist hard determinism, and machine reductionism critique contrasted with humanistic holism; balanced conclusion weighing scientific credibility against ecological validity."},{"id":"B3","min":7,"max":9,"descriptor":"Reasonably thorough and mostly accurate knowledge of the cognitive approach covering assumptions, schemas and at least one theoretical model; some detail but less depth or organisation than top band. Evaluation is reasonable and generally balanced, with at least two evaluation points, at least one of which is a comparison with another approach; points are explained but may lack development or full linkage to the description. Terminology mostly accurate; some attempt at overall discussion.","examples":"e.g. Correct outline of schema and inference, with one model (e.g. multi-store) described but not fully elaborated; evaluation includes machine reductionism and a comparison with the behaviourist approach, but points are asserted rather than developed; limited or no explicit conclusion."},{"id":"B2","min":4,"max":6,"descriptor":"Basic or superficial knowledge of the cognitive approach; assumptions and/or schema described with limited accuracy or detail; theoretical models mentioned but not explained, or only one feature covered. Evaluation is limited or generic (e.g. 'it is scientific', 'it lacks validity') with little elaboration; comparison with other approaches may be present but superficial or inaccurate. Discussion is disjointed; little or no attempt at overall judgement.","examples":"e.g. Mentions 'mind works like a computer' without unpacking; schema defined vaguely; evaluation limited to 'it is reductionist' with no explanation of what is reduced or why that matters; brief or inaccurate comparison with behaviourism."},{"id":"B1","min":1,"max":3,"descriptor":"Very limited, fragmentary or largely inaccurate knowledge of the cognitive approach; features may be listed without understanding (e.g. 'schemas, models, neuroscience' with no elaboration). Communication lacks organisation and accurate terminology.","examples":"e.g. One or two isolated accurate statements (e.g. 'schemas are mental structures'); evaluation absent or a single unsupported assertion; no comparison or an incorrect one (e.g. comparing cognitive approach to itself)."},{"id":"B0","min":0,"max":0,"descriptor":"No creditable material; response not worthy of credit.","examples":"e.g. No relevant content; restates the question; writes only about another approach with no cognitive content."}],"guidance":"Marks are awarded for the quality of the whole discussion, not for counting discrete points. Examiners judge the best fit across AO1 (description of assumptions, schemas, theoretical models, cognitive neuroscience) and AO3 (evaluation including comparison with other approaches). A response cannot reach the top band without at least two developed evaluation points, at least one being a comparison with another approach. Balance and organisation matter: a one-sided or purely descriptive answer is capped at Band 3. Accurate use of terminology (inference, schema, mediation, reductionism, determinism) supports higher bands but is not sufficient alone. Do not penalise omission of cognitive neuroscience if the rest is thorough, but its accurate inclusion strengthens AO1."},"answer":"Banded 12-mark discussion (AO1 description of the cognitive approach including schemas and theoretical models; AO3 evaluation including comparison with other approaches). Award the band whose descriptor best fits the whole response; marks within a band reflect how securely the response sits in that band.","acceptableAlternatives":["Any accurate theoretical model accepted (multi-store, working memory, levels of processing, cognitive priming, Beck's negative triad/Ellis's ABC) provided it is explained as a cognitive framework, not merely named","Comparison may be with behaviourist, social learning, psychodynamic, humanistic or biological approaches; any valid dimension (determinism, reductionism, scientific status, nature/nurture, application) is creditable","Evaluation via application (e.g. CBT, AI, eyewitness testimony research) is creditable where its evaluative force is explicit"],"commonMistakes":["Describing the approach with no evaluation, or evaluation with no description","Listing models by name without explaining what they show about mental processes","Confusing schema with 'scheme' or treating it as a behaviourist concept","Comparing the cognitive approach only with itself or with a mischaracterised other approach (e.g. claiming behaviourism denies all internal events)","Asserting 'reductionist' or 'deterministic' without explaining the sense (machine reductionism; soft determinism)","Omitting any overall judgement or conclusion in an otherwise strong answer"]}]}
